title: BNP and NT-proBNP
subtitle: Heart-failure likelihood, confounders and referral thresholds
summary: Heart-failure likelihood, confounders and referral thresholds
introduction: Natriuretic peptides support assessment of heart failure but do not independently diagnose congestion. Interpret with symptoms, ECG, examination, renal function, rhythm, age, obesity and echocardiography.

rows.name: <400 ng/L
rows.referenceRange: NICE chronic-HF referral category remains <400 ng/L. RVH laboratory guidance separately states NT-proBNP <125 ng/L excludes heart failure as a cause of signs/symptoms.
notes: Review alternative diagnoses, but levels can be lower with obesity or medications such as diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs/ARNI, beta blockers or mineralocorticoid antagonists.

rows.name: 400–2,000 ng/L
rows.referenceRange: NICE: specialist assessment and echocardiography within 6 weeks
notes: Does not prove heart failure. Renal impairment, AF, age, PE, sepsis and pulmonary hypertension can elevate the result.

rows.name: >2,000 ng/L
rows.referenceRange: NICE: urgent specialist assessment and echocardiography within 2 weeks
notes: Higher values are associated with worse prognosis, but acute disposition still depends on current symptoms and physiology.

urgentFindings: Breathlessness at rest, SpO₂ below expected range, inability to lie flat, pink frothy sputum, widespread crackles, hypotension or new confusion.
Rapidly increasing peripheral oedema with reduced urine output, chest pain or syncope.
Do not use a chronically raised BNP/NT-proBNP alone as evidence of acute fluid overload; compare with symptoms, examination, weight and previous results.
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.

commonPatterns.title: Heart failure effectively excluded by a low result
findings: NT-proBNP <400 ng/L (or <125 ng/L per RVH laboratory guidance for excluding HF as the cause of current signs/symptoms)
Breathlessness or oedema present, prompting the test
interpretation: A low result makes heart failure an unlikely explanation for the current symptoms and should prompt review of alternative diagnoses (respiratory, renal, venous, deconditioning)

Obesity and several heart-failure medications (diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs/ARNI, beta blockers, mineralocorticoid antagonists) can lower the result, so a low value in a treated patient needs cautious interpretation
actions: Review the medication list and body habitus before treating the result as fully reassuring
Investigate alternative causes of breathlessness or oedema (see further testing)
Safety-net and arrange follow-up if symptoms persist or worsen despite a low result

commonPatterns.title: Intermediate result — confounder review needed
findings: One or more of: renal impairment, atrial fibrillation, older age, possible PE, sepsis or pulmonary hypertension
interpretation: This range does not prove heart failure — several common confounders raise NT-proBNP independently of cardiac filling pressure
Still requires the NICE-recommended specialist assessment and echocardiography pathway even when a confounder is identified
actions: Check renal function and rhythm, and consider PE and sepsis as alternative or contributing explanations (see further testing)
Arrange specialist assessment and echocardiography within the NICE-recommended 6-week window
Manage current symptoms and physiology on their own merits rather than waiting for the echocardiogram if the patient is acutely unwell

commonPatterns.title: High result — urgent heart-failure pathway
interpretation: Associated with a higher likelihood of heart failure and worse prognosis, but the level itself does not determine whether the patient needs acute treatment today — that depends on current symptoms and physiology
A very high result in a patient who looks acutely unwell should not be treated as a routine referral
actions: Assess current symptoms and observations for acute decompensation and treat as time-critical if present (see urgent findings)
Arrange urgent specialist assessment and echocardiography within the NICE-recommended 2-week window if not acutely unwell
Compare with any previous NT-proBNP result to judge whether this represents a new rise or a known chronic elevation

commonPatterns.title: Chronic elevation vs acute decompensation
findings: NT-proBNP raised, but similar to a previous known result
No new breathlessness at rest, hypoxia, orthopnoea or examination change
interpretation: Chronically raised natriuretic peptides are expected in established heart failure, CKD and structural heart disease and do not by themselves indicate acute fluid overload
A rise from the patient's own known baseline is more informative than the absolute value in isolation
actions: Compare against previous results, current weight, examination and functional status rather than acting on the absolute value alone
Reassess urgently if there is any new breathlessness, hypoxia, inability to lie flat or examination change (see urgent findings)
Continue routine heart-failure management/follow-up if the patient is at their known baseline

rationale: Required to confirm or refute heart failure and characterise the underlying structural/functional abnormality once NT-proBNP has flagged the need for specialist assessment
Renal impairment is a common confounder that raises NT-proBNP independently of cardiac filling pressure, and is also needed before starting/titrating heart-failure medication
Identifies atrial fibrillation and other rhythm or ischaemic changes that can raise NT-proBNP or point to an alternative/contributing diagnosis
Supports assessment for an acute coronary or myocardial injury component when a raised natriuretic peptide occurs with chest pain or acute decompensation
Helps distinguish pulmonary oedema from a respiratory cause of breathlessness such as infection or effusion when the natriuretic peptide result is equivocal
Relevant when pulmonary embolism is a differential explanation for a raised NT-proBNP with breathlessness or hypoxia

specimens.notes: NT-proBNP: plasma — green-top lithium-heparin tube with yellow insert, 3 mL.
